strengths: Accurately frames the problem as retaining, replaying, controlling, and securing independently executing sub-agent runs rather than merely calling sub-agents and summarizing results.

Provides a strong core architecture: parent-side run registration, child-side run mapping, stable run identifiers, independent child context, event envelopes, replay, deduplication, cancellation, cleanup, access control, and background runs.
Covers both model-selected agent tools and command-style/programmatic entry points, including final tool-result contracts for success, validation failure, error, abort, and interruption.

Gives concrete state-machine and concurrency mechanisms, including CAS transitions, idempotent startup, unique keys, sequence handling, live/replay duplicate suppression, ordering among sibling runs, and max-concurrency rejection.

Handles edge cases called out by the request: duplicate requests, parallel execution, page refresh and reconnect, direct drill-in access, cancellation semantics, cleanup/tombstones, and runs with no direct parent tool call.
weaknesses: The solution is somewhat over-specified as a concrete framework design, including table names, field lists, implementation identifiers, and adapter names; this is mostly useful, but some details read closer to implementation architecture than patent-claim-level necessary features.

The causal technical-effect discussion is present throughout but not separately synthesized as strongly as the mechanism sections; effects are mostly implicit from the proposed state, replay, and control mechanisms.

A few implementation-specific names and capabilities are asserted as if they are existing framework facts rather than framed only as optional implementation choices, which creates minor support risk if the project snapshot did not contain them.

The live-tail reattachment fallback is conservative but leaves one branch where continued child execution may no longer be visible to the parent, so the recovery policy could be tightened for complete observability.
missing_key_mechanisms: A more explicit normalized retention policy matrix for different terminal states, storage quotas, and retention durations would strengthen the cleanup/保留 portion, though the core cleanup mechanism is already present.

A clearer account of how parent LLM context is bounded when many child chunks are visible to the user but only summaries or structured outputs are returned to the parent model would further strengthen the parent-model integration boundary.
A more direct technical-effect section tying each mechanism to each effect would improve disclosure readability, although the causal links are mostly inferable.
unsupported_claims: The artifact refers to existing or framework-specific constructs such as subAgent(Cls,name), runAgentTool, agentTool, UIMessageChunk, saveMessages, Think class agent, AIChatAgent, and child facet behavior. These may be valid if present in the provided project snapshot, but within the evaluated text they are sometimes stated as existing framework semantics rather than purely proposed implementation variants.

The proposed logical table names cf_agent_tool_runs and cf_agent_tool_child_runs are framed as possible implementations, so they are not unsupported facts; they are not treated as material unsupported claims.
score_rationale: This is a strong technical-solution answer aligned with the high end of the rubric. It identifies the real problem precisely: sub-agents must become retained, observable, recoverable, access-controlled execution entities rather than ordinary tool calls. Its core concept matches and extends the reference path through parent-side registration, child-side mapping, stable run identity, independent execution context, event bridge, replay/deduplication, access gate, cancellation, cleanup, concurrency, and background runs. The technical means are detailed and mostly necessary: idempotent startup with unique run IDs and CAS, event envelopes with sequence and replay flags, reducer-side deduplication and gap handling, state-machine terminal authority, parent-tool return contracts, drill-in authorization, cancellation separate from observation disconnects, and tombstone-style cleanup. This exceeds the reference mechanism depth and squarely addresses the request's hidden edge cases. I did not apply the score caps because the solution has an explicit parent registry, recovery and replay deduplication, cancellation/failure/cleanup handling, and access control. The score is not perfect mainly because some framework-specific names are asserted as existing facts rather than carefully qualified from the project snapshot, and because the disclosure is slightly implementation-heavy with a less concise technical-effect synthesis.
